title: The Change of Qiblah
subtitle: From Bayt al-Maqdis to the Ancient Kaaba and the Identity of the Median Community
summary: Sixteen months of facing Jerusalem in prayer, the Prophet's longing gaze toward the heavens, the revelation of Surah Al-Baqarah during midday prayer at Masjid al-Qiblatayn, the seamless rotation of the congregation, and the theological establishment of the Abrahamic spiritual center.

sections.text: For the first sixteen or seventeen months following the Hijrah to Madinah, the Muslim community directed their faces in every prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis—the sacred sanctuary of Jerusalem. During their earlier Makkan period, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ had tactfully combined both sanctuaries, praying on the southern side of the Kaaba so that both the ancient cube and Jerusalem lay in a direct alignment before him. In Madinah, however, which lay geographically situated directly between Makkah to the south and Jerusalem to the north, facing one sanctuary necessitated turning one's back directly upon the other.

Praying toward Jerusalem held profound theological resonance, emphasizing the continuity of divine revelation and honoring the sanctuary of prophets like Dawood, Sulayman, and Isa. Yet, it also created theological polemics in Madinah. Certain factions among the Jewish tribes argued that Muhammad and his followers had to copy their sacred direction because they lacked independent spiritual legitimacy, boasting: 'Muhammad opposes us in our ways, yet follows our Qiblah!'
The ancient Kaaba in Makkah, the primordial sanctuary of Ibrahim, toward which the Prophet's heart yearned.

In his heart, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ yearned deeply to face the Kaaba in Makkah—the primordial House of God built by the patriarch of monotheism, Ibrahim, and his son Isma'il. It was the Qiblah of his father Ibrahim, free from all sectarian claims. Yet, being the epitome of spiritual discipline, he never presumed to alter the prayer direction on his own initiative or utter an impatient complaint; instead, he would frequently step outside into the night and gaze silently toward the celestial canopy, awaiting divine command.

In the middle of Sha'ban in the second year after the Hijrah (February 624 CE), as the Prophet was leading the believers in prayer (traditionally reported as the Dhuhr or Asr prayer among the Banu Salamah clan at the site later known as Masjid al-Qiblatayn), the long-awaited divine decree descended through the Angel Jibril:

قَدْ نَرَىٰ تَقَلُّبَ وَجْهِكَ فِي السَّمَاءِ ۖ فَلَنُوَلِّيَنَّكَ قِبْلَةً تَرْضَاهَا ۚ فَوَلِّ وَجْهَكَ شَطْرَ الْمَسْجِدِ الْحَرَامِ ۚ وَحَيْثُ مَا كُنتُمْ فَوَلُّوا وُجُوهَكُمْ شَطْرَهُ
'We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven, and We will surely turn you to a qiblah with which you will be pleased. So turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram. And wherever you [believers] are, turn your faces toward it [in prayer].' (Surah Al-Baqarah 2:144)

Upon receiving the revelation mid-prayer, the Prophet ﷺ did not pause the service. Without an instant's hesitation, he turned one hundred and eighty degrees in mid-prayer from north to south, and the entire congregation behind him—men, women, and rows of worshippers—shifted seamlessly in complete synchronization, completing the remainder of their prayer facing the Kaaba in Makkah.

News of the change spread across the settlements of Madinah. At Masjid Quba the following morning during the Fajr prayer, a messenger arrived and called out through the window: 'Indeed, revelation has descended upon the Messenger of God tonight commanding him to face the Kaaba!' As recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari, the worshippers were bowing in Ruku' facing Jerusalem; hearing the announcement, the entire congregation rotated on their feet mid-prayer toward the Kaaba. This unhesitating submission demonstrated the believers' unshakeable obedience to divine command.
The serene architecture of early Madinan mosques where prayer united hearts across horizons.
The Median Community and Spiritual Independence

The change of Qiblah served as a profound divine sorting mechanism, separating sincere faith from superficial allegiance. Hypocrites and skeptics immediately objected, asking: 'What has turned them from their Qiblah which they used to face?' God revealed the comprehensive answer in Surah Al-Baqarah:

قُل لِّلَّهِ الْمَشْرِقُ وَالْمَغْرِبُ ۚ يَهْدِي مَن يَشَاءُ إِلَىٰ صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ * وَكَذَٰلِكَ جَعَلْنَاكُمْ أُمَّةً وَسَطًا لِّتَكُونُوا شُهَدَاءَ عَلَى النَّاسِ
'Say: To God belongs the east and the west. He guides whom He wills to a straight path. And thus We have made you a median community that you will be witnesses over the people...' (Surah Al-Baqarah 2:142–143)

By redirecting their prayers toward the ancient sanctuary of Makkah, the Muslim community affirmed its independent theological identity. They were not an offshoot of earlier religious sects, but the direct inheritors of the pure, primordial monotheism of Ibrahim. Facing the Kaaba united believers across every continent into a single spiritual focal point, anchoring the community for the epic trials that lay immediately ahead.
